big_idea: Sharing fairly between 2 friends gives halves; between 4 gives fourths. One half equals two fourths.
learning_intention: We are learning to share fairly between 2 or 4 friends and see that one half equals two fourths of the same whole.
student_learning_goal: I can share a small collection fairly between 2 or 4 friends, draw the share, and tell that one half equals two fourths.
success_criteria: I can share a collection fairly between 2 or 4 friends.
I can draw the share with leftovers if there are any.
I can show that 1/2 = 2/4 of the same pizza.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Halves and Fourths' showing a circle whole, a circle in halves, a circle in fourths

OPTIONAL: Lila and Otto — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
5 large paper-pizza demos (whole, halved, fourthed, sixthed, eighthed)
Lesson 5 formative tracker (Fair Shares + Fractions) — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Otto baked one pizza. 2 friends are coming over. How does he cut it? Scoot pops in with Lila + Otto: 'Fair shares are FRIENDLY shares!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Otto and a paper pizza (whole).

'Friends — Otto baked a pizza for his party. Two friends are coming over. He wants to share it FAIRLY. Watch.' Cut the pizza in half (or fold and tear it). Hold up the two pieces. 'Two pieces. Same SIZE. We call this a HALF. Each friend gets ONE HALF — written 1/2.' Write 1/2 on the chart.

'But wait — Otto has another pizza. This time FOUR friends are coming.' Hold up another pizza. Cut into fourths. 'Four pieces, same size. Each piece is a FOURTH — written 1/4. Each friend gets 1/4.'

'Now here's a question. Otto's first pizza was cut in HALVES. His second was cut in FOURTHS. Are these two pieces the same?' Hold up one HALF and TWO FOURTHS together. Children's eyes will go to the comparison. 'Watch.' Lay the half on top of the two fourths. They cover the same area exactly. 'ONE HALF equals TWO FOURTHS of the same pizza! These are different ways to write the SAME amount.' Write 1/2 = 2/4 on the chart.

'Today we're going to be Fair-Share Detectives. We'll share collections of buttons or counters between 2 friends OR 4 friends. We'll see that 1/2 and 2/4 are equal. And we'll learn how to compare unit fractions like 1/2, 1/3, 1/4.'
student_actions: Help write the 1/2 = 2/4 equation on the chart.
Predict what 1/3 of a pizza would look like.

steps.instruction:
WHOLE GROUP RECAP — 5 min — four 60-second mini-stations on the carpet, each mirroring one prior day:
  Station 1 (D1 — Count Big): Lila holds up a 10-rod, class counts on by 10s to 50.
  Station 2 (D2 — Read and Show): Otto writes '37' on the chart, class shows it with rods (3 tens + 7 ones).
  Station 3 (D3 — Make and Break): Lila says '50', class breaks it two ways (e.g. 30+20 or 40+10).
  Station 4 (D4 — Compare and Order): Otto holds 24 vs 42, class says which is greater AND how they decided.
Each named skill recall sets up today's fair-shares work.
steps.teacher_prompt: Lila + Otto: 'You can COUNT big, READ numbers, MAKE+BREAK 50, and COMPARE pairs. Today's fair-shares lesson uses ALL FOUR.'

steps.instruction: Send children to small groups of 4. Each group gets 4 paper plates and 12 paper buttons. Round 1: 'Share these 12 buttons fairly between 2 friends.' Children deal one at a time onto two plates. Check (6 each).
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Round 1 — share 12 buttons between 2 friends. How will you make it fair? Show me.' Walk around. Some children scoop 6 at once; nudge them to use the deal-one-at-a-time strategy.

steps.instruction: Round 2: 'Share 12 buttons fairly between 4 friends.' (3 each.) Then Round 3 (the leftover round): 'Share 13 buttons fairly between 2 friends.' (6 each + 1 leftover.) Round 4: 'Share 14 buttons fairly between 4 friends.' (3 each + 2 leftover.)
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Now share 12 between 4 friends.' (3 each.) 'Now 13 between 2 — what happens?' Children discover the leftover. 'What can we do with the 1 leftover button? Cut it in half? Put it back in Otto's box? Save for later?' Validate any plausible plan. Then 14 between 4. (3 each + 2 leftover.)

steps.instruction: Pizza fraction reveal. Bring children back to the carpet. Hold up the halved pizza and the fourthed pizza side by side. Lay one half on top of two fourths to show equivalence. Discuss: 'Same size, different number of pieces.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Let's check this fraction trick again.' Lay a half on two fourths. 'Same. So 1/2 = 2/4.' Then ask: 'What about a half and THREE fourths? Is that the same?' (No — three fourths is BIGGER.) 'And one half and ONE fourth?' (No — one fourth is SMALLER.) Build the rule: 'Equivalent fractions have the same area. Different fractions cover different areas.'

steps.instruction: Unit Fraction Sort. Each pair gets cards showing 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8 of the same pizza. They sort from BIGGEST share to SMALLEST share. The reveal: more sharers means smaller pieces.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You have six fraction cards. ALL show different shares of the SAME pizza. Sort them from BIGGEST piece to SMALLEST piece.' Children typically sort 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8 correctly because they SEE the pieces visually. Discuss: 'Which has the BIGGER number on the bottom — 1/2 or 1/8?' (1/8.) 'Which is the BIGGER PIECE?' (1/2.) 'Bigger denominator means SMALLER piece.'

steps.instruction: Closing summative artifact: hand out the Fair-Share + Fraction worksheet. Children complete it independently. Teacher records the formative tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You've shared a lot today and you've seen halves and fourths. Last thing — a worksheet to show what you learned. Three parts. Take your time.' Distribute. Walk around. Tick each child's row on the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: These children focus on Round 1 and Round 2 (no leftovers). The dealing strategy is the focus; leftover reasoning comes once that's solid. Skip the unit fraction sort for these children.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch round: 'Share 25 buttons between 4 friends — what happens?' (6 each + 1 leftover.) Or: 'Share a pizza into SIXTHS. Then into TWELFTHS. What's 1/6 = ?/12?' Stays inside B1.6/B1.8 with stretch into Grade 2 fraction equivalence.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Use the chant 'one for you, one for me' during dealing. Provide a fraction-picture reference card (1/2, 1/3, 1/4 visually). Allow physical demonstration of the half-equals-two-fourths overlay.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Acted-out version: children form groups of 2 or 4 and physically share a 'pizza' (paper plate). The dealing rhythm and the size-comparison are embodied.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Does the child deal one at a time? Can they articulate the leftover plan? Can they SEE that 1/2 = 2/4 (unprompted)? Can they sort unit fractions from biggest to smallest piece?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the tracker per child. The 'recognises 1/2 = 2/4' and 'orders unit fractions correctly' columns are the B1.7 and B1.8 mastery signals.
tracker_columns: Orders unit fractions biggest to smallest

discussion_prompts: What's one thing in your house that gets shared fairly?
If a pizza has 4 slices and you eat 2, what fraction did you eat?
Which is more: 1/2 of a pizza or 1/4 of a pizza? How do you know?
Why does 1/8 mean a SMALLER piece even though 8 is a bigger number than 4?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child whispers to a partner: '1/2 of a pizza is the SAME as ___ /4.' Partners answer: 'two-fourths!' Then the class chants: '1/2 = 2/4!' Children pack up the manipulatives and line up at the door. Scoot's capstone send-off: 'Halves, fourths — Scoot says: math is FRIENDS!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Fair Shares + Fractions tracker for B1.6/B1.7/B1.8. Summative worksheet artifact (3 parts).
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 5 is the SUMMATIVE artifact for the unit. B1.6 (fair share with leftovers), B1.7 (1/2 = 2/4 equivalence), and B1.8 (unit fraction comparison) all live or die on this lesson. The tracker captures all three skills explicitly.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says 1/4 is bigger than 1/2 — repairing the bigger-number-bigger-piece confusion
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: The most common Grade-1 trap on B1.8 is the child who says 1/4 > 1/2 because '4 is bigger than 2'. This is the WHOLE-NUMBER intuition transferred to fractions, where it fails. Children's K experience says bigger numbers mean bigger things; fractions invert this for the denominator. The repair must be VISUAL — the pizza overlay is the conceptual centre. Step 3 (pizza fraction reveal) is where this surfaces. The script below covers what to say when the child INSISTS that 1/4 is bigger.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at the unit fraction sort. They've sorted the cards as: 1/2, 1/4, 1/3, 1/5, 1/8, 1/6 — clearly broken. They put 1/4 BEFORE 1/3 because 4 > 3. The teacher walks up.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the pair. 'Tell me about your sort.' The child says 'we put bigger numbers first'. 'Hmm. Let me show you something.' Pick up the 1/2 card and the 1/4 card. Lay them on the carpet. 'Which PIECE is bigger?' Wait. Some children point at 1/2 (looking at the visual); some still say 1/4 (looking at the number).

If they say 1/4: 'Lay them on top of each other. Look at the SIZE.' The 1/4 piece visibly fits inside the 1/2 piece. 'Which piece COVERS more pizza?' (1/2.) 'Which piece would you rather eat if you were really hungry?' (1/2.) 'Right — 1/2 is the BIGGER PIECE even though 4 is a bigger NUMBER.'

'Watch what happens when more friends share.' Hold up 1/2 (2 friends share a pizza). 'Lila and Otto share 1 pizza. Each gets 1/2.' Hold up 1/4 (4 friends share). 'Now 4 friends share. Each gets 1/4. With more friends, each piece gets SMALLER.'

'So the rule is: MORE friends sharing = SMALLER pieces. The bottom number tells us how MANY friends. If the bottom is 8, that's 8 friends sharing — each piece is TINY.' Write the rule on the chart: 'BIGGER bottom number = SMALLER piece.'

Resort with the child: 1/2 (biggest), 1/3, 1/4, 1/5, 1/6, 1/8 (smallest). Tick 'orders unit fractions correctly' on the tracker.

If the child STILL flips back to whole-number reasoning: send them home with a parent note encouraging fraction comparisons at meals (more siblings sharing a pie = smaller slices). The intuition needs repeated context.

Long-term recovery: this misconception is so common it's worth a class poster. 'BIGGER bottom = SMALLER piece' should hang on the wall through the end of the year.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Says 1/4 > 1/2 because 4 > 2. Whole-number rule transferred. Most common Grade-1 starting point.
(Mid) After the overlay demo, says 1/2 > 1/4 but flips again on 1/3 vs 1/4. The bigger-bottom-smaller-piece rule isn't yet consistent.
(Strong) Sorts unit fractions biggest-piece to smallest-piece without prompting. Articulates 'more friends sharing = smaller pieces'.
(Stretched) Volunteers: 'I bet 1/100 would be a TINY piece — 100 friends sharing one pizza!' Has generalised the rule beyond the unit-fraction set.
common_misconceptions: Bigger denominator = bigger piece. (Whole-number intuition. Repair: physical overlay of pizza pieces.)
Numerators and denominators are independent. (Children sometimes fixate on just the top or just the bottom. Repair: keep numerator at 1 in this lesson; introduce non-unit fractions later.)
All fractions are 'less than 1'. (True for unit fractions and proper fractions; not for fractions like 5/4. Don't introduce improper fractions in Grade 1.)
recovery_moves: Always use the pizza overlay. Visual proof beats verbal explanation. Stack 1/2 on top of two 1/4 pieces; show they cover the same area.
Connect to sharing context. 'More friends sharing the same pizza = each gets a smaller piece.' This grounds the abstract rule in lived experience.
Use 'bigger bottom = smaller piece' as a class chant. Rhythmic verbal reinforcement is more durable than a single demo at K-G1.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice and summative evidence of B1.6 (fair sharing with leftovers), B1.7 (1/2 = 2/4 equivalence), B1.8 (unit fraction comparison).

parts_outline.task: Two fair-share scenes. Scene A: 12 buttons, 4 plates. Scene B: 13 buttons, 4 plates. Child draws each share, circles any leftover, and writes the count per plate.

Pizza equivalence. A pizza halved and a pizza fourthed are shown side by side. The child colours 1/2 of one pizza and 2/4 of the other to show they cover the same area, then writes the equation 1/2 = 2/4.
Unit fraction comparison: four pizza pictures showing 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/5 of the same whole. Child orders them from BIGGEST piece to SMALLEST piece by drawing a line connecting them.
